actions.justification: Mandatory initial assessment of vital signs to establish baseline and monitor for hemodynamic instability in this COPD exacerbation patient.
Mandatory assessment of respiratory status including breath sounds, work of breathing, and degree of obstruction — critical for COPD exacerbation evaluation.
Mandatory arterial blood gas to evaluate for hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis, which are key determinants of COPD exacerbation severity and need for NIV.
MANDATORY action - chest X-ray is required within 60 minutes to evaluate for pneumonia, pneumothorax, hyperinflation, or other causes of worsening dyspnea in this COPD patient.
Mental status assessment is critical in COPD exacerbation to evaluate for hypercapnic encephalopathy and to determine eligibility for NIV vs. intubation, despite currently stable vitals.
COPD exacerbation guidelines recommend early assessment of NIV eligibility. Patient has known COPD with worsening dyspnea; NIV can reduce intubation risk and mortality if indicated.
COPD exacerbation with increased sputum suggests possible infectious trigger; blood culture should be obtained before initiating antibiotics to identify causative organism.
Short-acting bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists/anticholinergics) are first-line treatment for COPD exacerbation to relieve bronchospasm and dyspnea per GOLD guidelines.
Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone) reduce airway inflammation and shorten recovery time in COPD exacerbations per GOLD guidelines.
CBC will help identify leukocytosis (infection/COPD exacerbation), anemia, or polycythemia relevant to this patient with COPD and worsening dyspnea.
BMP is critical given the patient's known AKI comorbidity — assess renal function, electrolytes, and acid-base status to guide management and medication dosing.
Patient with COPD exacerbation and AKI warrants pulmonology input for specialist guidance on NIV, bronchodilator titration, and further workup of worsening dyspnea.

Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral exacerbation of COPD, guiding antibiotic decision-making. This patient presents with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum, consistent with possible COPD exacerbation with infectious etiology.
Sputum culture is essential in COPD exacerbation with increased sputum production to identify causative organism and guide targeted antibiotic therapy before empiric antibiotics are started.

Lactate assessment is warranted given the patient has AKI as a comorbidity and worsening respiratory status; elevated lactate would indicate tissue hypoperfusion or respiratory failure severity, and helps guide management.

Patient with COPD and worsening dyspnea warrants CT chest to evaluate for pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or other structural causes not fully characterized by plain chest X-ray (already completed). CT provides more detailed anatomical information to guide diagnosis and treatment.

Despite SpO2 of 98%, the patient has COPD with worsening dyspnea. Controlled supplemental oxygen should be administered cautiously to maintain SpO2 at target 88-92% per COPD guidelines, avoiding hypercapnic drive suppression while ensuring adequate oxygenation.

Patient presents with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production consistent with COPD exacerbation, likely infectious etiology. Blood cultures are pending (already ordered). Antibiotic therapy is indicated for COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum per GOLD guidelines. Initiating now after cultures were already ordered.

Patient has AKI as a comorbidity and is hemodynamically stable. Cautious IV fluid administration is appropriate to support renal perfusion and prevent further AKI progression in the setting of COPD exacerbation. Vasopressors are not indicated given adequate MAP, and diuretics are not indicated without evidence of fluid overload.

Patient with COPD and AKI presenting with worsening dyspnea may have a fluid overload component. Given stable vitals (SpO2 98%, HR 80, BP 120/80) and the AHA heart failure guideline context, cautious diuresis may help relieve dyspnea if fluid overload is contributing, while monitoring renal function given underlying AKI.

The only available action in this phase. Patient has COPD exacerbation with AKI comorbidity. Current MAP is 103 and vitals are stable, so vasopressor is not urgently indicated, but it is the only action available and should be held ready given AKI risk and potential hemodynamic compromise. Selecting as the sole available action to progress the clinical decision pathway.
Patient has AKI as comorbidity; IV fluids and antibiotics have been given, so serial renal function monitoring is essential to track AKI trajectory and adjust medications accordingly.

Serial reassessment of respiratory status is required after bronchodilator and corticosteroid administration to evaluate treatment response and determine if NIV initiation or escalation is needed per GOLD COPD guidelines.
Patient has AKI comorbidity and received IV fluids and diuretics; monitoring fluid balance is essential to avoid fluid overload or worsening renal function.
